cards.title: Introduction to Client-Side Routing
cards.content:
In traditional multi-page applications, every navigation request results in the browser requesting a completely new HTML document from the server. This causes a full page reload.

In modern Single Page Applications (SPAs) built with React, we use Client-Side Routing. Instead of requesting a new page from the server, a client-side router intercepts browser navigation, updates the URL bar dynamically, and renders the corresponding component inside the existing document without a reload.

options.text: Client-side routing requires a full page refresh for every navigation action.
Client-side routing updates the URL and changes the DOM view instantly without requesting a new HTML page from the server.
Server-side routing is faster because it does not require JavaScript to load.

cards.title: Configuring React Router v6
cards.content:
To enable routing in a React app, we use the react-router-dom library. We must first wrap our root component with BrowserRouter to enable routing context.

Inside, we declare individual routes using the Routes wrapper and individual Route components.

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route path='/' element={<Home />} />
        <Route path='/about' element={<About />} />
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

cards.title: Navigating with Link and NavLink
cards.content:
Do not use standard HTML <a href='...'> tags for internal links! Using them causes a hard page reload, losing your application's state.

Instead, React Router provides two replacement components:

  • <Link to='/about'>: Performs standard client-side navigation.
  • <NavLink to='/about'>: Special version of Link that automatically adds an active class or styles when the current route matches the URL.

cards.title: Dynamic Routing & Path Parameters
cards.content:
Frequently, pages must render dynamic content based on identifiers (like a user ID or product slug). We define these parameters in the route configuration using a colon (:) prefix.

<Route path='/user/:userId' element={<UserProfile />} />

Within the rendered component, we extract this dynamic parameter using the useParams hook:

import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';

function UserProfile() {
  const { userId } = useParams();
  return <h1>User Profile ID: {userId}</h1>;
}

cards.title: Summary & Best Practices
cards.content:
Congratulations! You have completed the foundation of routing in React. Let's recap key takeaways:

  • Keep it Declarative: Define routes cleanly inside structured Route elements.
  • Prevent Reloads: Always use Link or NavLink instead of anchor tags.
  • Dynamic Context: Utilize hooks like useParams and useNavigate to hook into route states.
  • Fallback Routes: Always establish a wildcard fallback route (path='*') to gracefully handle broken links or missing paths.
